hints.junior: One function, a whole library. The bundler didn't remove the rest because it genuinely couldn't prove that was safe.
hints.mid: Without a signal, the bundler assumes module-level code might have side effects and keeps it, on purpose.
hints.staff: Tree shaking is a proof problem: unreachable AND side-effect-free, and JS's dynamism makes that proof hard by default.

hints.junior: Same one-function import, two very different bundle sizes, toggle to see why.
hints.mid: The import statement never changes, only the library's own sideEffects field does.
hints.staff: Entirely a build-time static-analysis difference, nothing about runtime behavior changes either way.

hints.junior: sideEffects: false is a promise from the library author that importing a file does nothing meaningful on its own.
hints.mid: List real side-effectful files explicitly instead of marking the whole package, everything not listed is fair game.
hints.staff: Only helps if the library ships real ES modules, static import/export is what makes this analysis possible at all.

hints.junior: Only mark a package side-effect-free if that's actually true, or you get a silent runtime bug, not a build error.
hints.mid: CSS imports are the most common accidental violation, they have a real side effect and need excluding explicitly.
hints.staff: Verify with a real bundle analyzer, a present-but-ineffective sideEffects field gives false confidence with zero benefit.

sections.junior: Hey! Today's case is about importing one function from a utility library, and watching the bundle grow by the size of the whole thing anyway.
sections.mid: Without an explicit signal, a bundler has to assume any module-level code might have a side effect — deleting code that might do that would be an unsafe optimization.
sections.staff: Tree shaking is fundamentally a proof problem — the bundler must prove an export is unreachable and side-effect-free before removing it, and JavaScript's dynamic nature makes that hard to construct automatically.

sections.junior: The fix is a single package.json field, sideEffects: false, telling the bundler it's safe to remove anything the app doesn't actually use.
sections.mid: If a package genuinely has a few side-effectful files, list them explicitly instead of marking the whole package — everything not listed is fair game for removal.
sections.staff: This only helps if the library is authored as real ES modules — static import and export syntax is what lets the bundler analyze reachability at all, a CommonJS require() graph is opaque to it.

sections.junior: Toggle between a library with no sideEffects field and one that declares itself safe, and watch the simulated bundle breakdown change.
sections.mid: The import statement in the app code never changes — only the library's own package.json field does.
sections.staff: This is entirely a build-time, static-analysis difference — nothing about runtime behavior changes either way.

sections.junior: Without a sideEffects signal, bundlers play it safe and keep everything. One field changes that.
sections.mid: sideEffects: false in package.json tells the bundler it's safe to remove any export the app doesn't use — list real side-effectful files explicitly rather than marking a whole package false.
sections.staff: Verify the reduction actually happened with a bundle analyzer, not just the config.
